title: Career Exploration: Interests, Strengths & Work Environments
summary: Learn how interests, strengths, preferred work environments, values, and experiences can help you explore careers without treating one assessment or preference as a final career decision.
objectives: Identify personal interests, strengths, values, and preferred work conditions.
Explain the difference between exploring a career and being qualified for that career.
Compare multiple career options before selecting a possible next step.

vocab.def: Learning about occupations, career families, work environments, requirements, and possible next steps.
A group of related occupations that share similar work, knowledge, skills, or environments.
An ability, skill, habit, or quality that can support effective performance.
The physical, social, organizational, and operational conditions in which work is performed.

sections.heading: Career planning starts with exploration
sections.body: You do not need to know your lifelong career immediately. Strong career planning begins by exploring different occupations and career families and learning how they compare.

sections.heading: Interests and strengths are clues, not commands
sections.body: Things you enjoy, skills you already have, and abilities you want to develop can help narrow possibilities, but no single interest survey or assessment should decide your career for you.

sections.heading: Work environment matters
sections.body: Two jobs can use similar skills while having very different schedules, workplaces, physical demands, levels of teamwork, customer interaction, technology use, or responsibility.

sections.heading: Exploring a career is not the same as being qualified
sections.body: Learning about an occupation or taking preparation coursework can help you understand a field, but actual qualification may require additional education, training, credentials, experience, licensure, employer selection, or other requirements.

practice.prompt: You enjoy solving technical problems and working with equipment. Does that automatically mean one specific career is the correct choice?
practice.answer: No. Those interests can guide exploration across multiple occupations and work environments.

practice.prompt: You complete an introductory course about a career. Does that automatically make you occupationally qualified?
practice.answer: No. Exploration and preparation are different from formal qualification, credentialing, or employment.

quiz.question: What is the strongest way to use your interests when planning a career?
options: Use them as one source of information while comparing multiple careers and requirements
Treat one interest result as a permanent career decision
Ignore work environment and job requirements
Assume interest alone proves job qualification
quiz.answer: Use them as one source of information while comparing multiple careers and requirements

lab.objective: Create a comparison of three simulated career options using interests, strengths, work environment, typical tasks, training expectations, and possible next steps.

reflectionPrompt: What matters most to you in a future work environment, and why should that be considered alongside your interests and strengths?
